claims.text: The as-deposited protective coating has a dual-phase microstructure containing coherent FCC and BCC regions.
Enhanced creep resistance under continuous loading is governed by impeded dislocation motion at coherent FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
Coherent FCC/BCC interfaces act as barriers to dislocation glide.
Coherent FCC/BCC interfaces impede dislocation climb.
Impeded dislocation motion produces localized dislocation pile-ups at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Localized dislocation pile-ups generate enhanced back stresses.
Enhanced back stresses reduce the coating's overall creep strain rate.
Lattice-parameter mismatch at coherent FCC/BCC boundaries promotes dislocation pile-up and limits dislocation climb across the interface.
Under continuous load, dislocations generated in the FCC phase must overcome a barrier posed by the BCC phase.
Impeded dislocation transfer creates localized stress concentrations and increases the need for dislocation climb.
Delayed dislocation motion lowers the coating's overall creep strain rate.
Relative to a comparable single-phase or homogenized HEA coating, the FCC/BCC coating will have a lower steady-state creep rate.
Relative to the control, the FCC/BCC coating will have greater resistance to progressive plastic deformation.
Creep deformation of the FCC/BCC coating will produce preferential dislocation accumulation at phase boundaries without significant recovery by climb or interface decohesion.
A comparable single-phase or homogenized HEA coating typically has a higher creep rate because dislocation motion is uninterrupted by FCC/BCC interfaces.
Thermal activation promotes creep at approximately 0.4–0.6 times the melting temperature.
The proposed interface-barrier mechanism operates below the melting point and phase-coarsening temperature but at temperatures high enough to activate creep.
